# The Pigmaleon Effect as Expectations Mold Results

The video explains the Pigmalion effect with the example of a teacher who treats an average student as a genius. It shows how the expectation changes the behavior of the teacher, creates self-efficacy in the student (the Galatean effect) and closes a cycle that confirms the initial expectation.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on September 3, 2026 (1 min 28 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5T0ZhmtShMU

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## Expectations mold results

According to the video, the Pigmalion effect shows that expectations create reality: talent is not fixed and adapts to what others project on the person [00:00].

## The cycle, step by step

The example is a teacher who believes that an average student is a genius [00:00]:

1. The expectation changes the behavior of the teacher: he dedicates more time, gives richer explanations and has more patience with the student [00:00].
2. More attention, alone, does not make the student smarter. Support needs to change the way students think about themselves [00:21].
3. Constant encouragement creates the conviction that he is capable of mastering matter. This is self-efficacy [00:21].
4. With this confidence, the student changes his posture: stop escaping from difficulties and try harder. It is the Galatean effect [00:44].
5. The effort generates excellent notes, which confirm the teacher's expectation and enhance the cycle [00:44].

In the end, the student who had average grades starts to lead the class, because the teacher chose to treat him as a genius [01:07].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between the Pigmalion effect and the Galatean effect?

In the video, the Pigmalion effect is the teacher's expectation changing the result. The Galatean effect is the change of posture of the student, when he comes to believe that he is capable [00:44].

### Is the teacher's attention enough?

Nope. Support needs to create in the student the conviction that he is capable, self-efficacy [00:21].
